meta.title: Who really said "An Epigram is Only a Wisecrack That’s Played Carnegie Hall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The line is Oscar Levant’s, not Edmund Fuller’s — Fuller was the editor who wrote it down. And Levant’s word was “gag,” not “wisecrack.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'An Epigram is Only a Wisecrack That’s Played Carnegie Hall'?
meta.ogDescription: Catalogued under its compiler, not its author. Oscar Levant said it; Edmund Fuller printed it in 1941; “wisecrack” replaced “gag” by 1949.

answer.label: Not Edmund Fuller — actually Oscar Levant
answer.authorDates: 1906–1972 · American concert pianist, composer, actor and professional wit
answer.sourceLine: Edmund Fuller did not write this line; he printed it. Fuller was the Crown Publishers editor whose Thesaurus of Quotations (1941) gives the earliest appearance Quote Investigator located — and it credits Oscar Levant, as every later citation does whenever anyone is credited at all. Fuller is one of the candidate names Quote Investigator opens its investigation with — and his own 1943 companion volume settles it by introducing the line as Levant’s. The wording drifted too: Levant’s recorded line is “a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall,” and “wisecrack” does not appear until 1949.

source.heading: The earliest printing, and the word that changed

docMeta.dd: Thesaurus of Quotations, ed. Edmund Fuller (1941), p. 331
“An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall”
Evan Esar, ed., The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949)
Disputed — right joke, wrong author, and one word changed

source.excerpt: What is an epigram? What sets it apart from the quip, the quiddity, the bon mot… It is Oscar Levant who has definitively scored it for our time with a fine sensitivity to the fact that stuffing is out of place in a humorist’s shirt. By Oscar, “An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall.”
trail: Quote Investigator dates the earliest instance to Edmund Fuller’s Thesaurus of Quotations (1941), p. 331, where the saying reads “An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall” and is attributed to Oscar Levant. Its conclusion: “All the cites credit the phrase to Oscar Levant whenever someone is credited” and “QI believes he is the most likely originator.”

Fuller’s 1943 Thesaurus of Epigrams introduces the line in his own prose as Levant’s — “By Oscar…” — which is the strongest single piece of evidence that the compiler never claimed it. The volume is catalogued as Thesaurus of Epigrams, Edmund Fuller, Crown, 1943: see the Internet Archive catalogue record.

The “wisecrack” form is a later substitution. Quote Investigator records it first in Bennett Cerf’s Laughing Stock (1945) as “a wise-crack that has played Carnegie Hall”, and then in exactly this page’s wording in Evan Esar’s The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949).

The joke depends on Levant being who he was. Wikipedia records him as a concert pianist who was for a time the highest-paid in the United States and a celebrated wit on the radio quiz show Information Please — a man who had genuinely played Carnegie Hall making a joke about what happens when a wisecrack does.

Wikiquote also carries the line for Levant, but in a weaker form: it gives the “wisecrack” wording with an “at” and cites Coronet magazine (September 1968) — twenty-seven years after Fuller’s printing. See the entry; we follow Quote Investigator’s earlier citation instead.

source.excerptNote: This is Fuller’s own framing, from his 1943 companion volume, and it settles the authorship question by itself: the editor most often credited with the line introduces it as Levant’s. Note the word — gag. Both passages are quoted as transcribed by Quote Investigator, which verified them on paper; the volumes are in copyright and we could not read them directly.

source.rightsNote: The earliest known printing is from 1941, well after the 1931 cutoff for the United States public domain, so this is treated as in copyright. We should be straight about the uncertainty: copyright in a 1941 or 1949 American book depended on renewal, and we did not search the renewal records, so we cannot say whether these particular volumes were renewed. Where the status is unresolved, the conservative reading is the one we publish. The single sentence is quoted for identification and criticism.

author.name: Oscar Levant
author.heading: About Oscar Levant
author.metaLine: 1906–1972 · American concert pianist, composer & professional wit
author.bio: Oscar Levant (1906–1972) was an American concert pianist, composer and actor who became, improbably, one of the best-known comedians of his era. Born in Pittsburgh and trained under Zygmunt Stojowski and Arnold Schoenberg, he was for a period in the 1940s the highest-paid concert pianist in the United States; he was also a fixture on the radio quiz show Information Please, where a one-off guest slot became a regular one because he proved so quick-witted and popular. He was close to George Gershwin, appeared in An American in Paris (1951) and The Band Wagon (1953), and wrote three books of mordant memoir, the first being A Smattering of Ignorance (1940).

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This line is a clean example of a particular filing error: the compiler of a quotation book inherits the quotations in it. Fuller recorded the joke and credited Levant on the page, and has been carrying the credit ever since.

items.why: Edmund Maybank Fuller (1914–2001) was an American editor, novelist, historian and critic who served eight years as editor-in-chief at Crown Publishers, where he compiled the large collections of quotations, anecdotes and epigrams this line first appeared in. His own 1943 volume introduces the saying as Levant’s. See his biography.

items.who: Levant — but not in these words
items.why: Levant’s line as first recorded in 1941 uses gag, not wisecrack. The swap appears in Bennett Cerf’s 1945 collection and Evan Esar’s 1949 dictionary, and it is the later version that became standard.

A 1965 Connecticut newspaper ran a further variant — “an epigram is a wisecrack that lived long enough to acquire a reputation” — with no attribution at all, the one unattributed reworking Quote Investigator records.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Oscar Levant’s. Edmund Fuller wrote it down in 1941 and said so on the page — and his word for it was “gag.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke only works if you know what Carnegie Hall meant, and it only lands if you know who was telling it. Levant was a serious concert pianist — for a stretch of the 1940s the best-paid in America — who became famous to a much larger public as the fastest man on a radio panel show. He was a wisecrack that had played Carnegie Hall.
That is the real content of the line: it is a definition of the epigram that quietly denies the epigram any dignity. A wisecrack and an epigram are the same joke; the difference is only the room.
detailsBody: Levant moved between the two worlds the joke describes. He studied with Arnold Schoenberg, recorded widely as a pianist, was close to George Gershwin and played himself in Gershwin’s biopic Rhapsody in Blue (1945), and took supporting roles in An American in Paris (1951) and The Band Wagon (1953). He also published three books of his own, beginning with A Smattering of Ignorance (1940).

Fuller’s framing in 1943 is worth keeping for its own sake: he introduces Levant as the man who “has definitively scored it for our time with a fine sensitivity to the fact that stuffing is out of place in a humorist’s shirt” — a compiler making the case that the wisecrack belongs in the anthology.
context.pull: A wisecrack and an epigram are the same joke. The difference is the room.

Oscar Levant (27 December 1906 – 14 August 1972) was an American concert pianist, composer and actor, for a period in the 1940s the highest-paid concert pianist in the US, and a regular wit on the radio quiz show Information Please.
Edmund Maybank Fuller (3 March 1914 – 29 January 2001) was an American educator, editor, novelist, historian and literary critic.
Thesaurus of Epigrams, by Edmund Fuller, was published by Crown in 1943.
Wikiquote’s Oscar Levant page carries the line as "An epigram is only a wisecrack that’s played at Carnegie Hall," cited to Coronet Magazine (September 1968).
